_comment: Canonical sound assets the game may reuse. `audio` points at the same file the audiobook plays: one generated effect, used in both places, never a second copy for Godot. Playback timing is NOT exported -- the audiobook's cue sheet times these against narration, and the game times them against gameplay. `generated` false means the asset is approved but not yet made.

assets.description: Categorised `alarm`, not `ambience`, so switching ambience off does not silence the chapter's alarm. Loops under the opening sequence and is ducked hard beneath speech.

The cheapest honest way to tell the listener Sarah is on a speaker and not in the room. It sits under her intercom lines without touching her approved voice clips, which are never filtered or regenerated for this.
Once Jack orders the settlement-wide emergency the sirens do not stop. Heard from inside, which is where both chapters stay.
The tension spine of the last third, and the beginning of the TOMBS Array's own sound identity. It enters when the remote initialization request appears and does not leave.

The one environmental bed for Chapter 1. The whole chapter is Jack's laboratory; there is no location change in the manuscript, so there is no second bed. Its prompt is deliberately terse: the first version was 476 characters and was rejected twice with HTTP 400, at 22 seconds and again at 20, while every other asset -- including a 20-second looping bed -- generated fine at 385 characters or fewer. The cause was prompt LENGTH, not duration. Nothing substantive was dropped, only words.
Used twice, before each Request denied. Hearing the same refusal twice is the information: Jack tried again and got nowhere.
Distinct from the denial tone on purpose. The story distinguishes being refused from being locked out, and that difference is the chapter's ending; it should not sound the same.
A single interruption, distinct from the polite chirp and from the full eruption. Used twice: the second alarm during the trace, and the tone that interrupts the couple much later.
The TOMBS Array's rings, the signature machine sound of chapter 2. Loops because the manuscript has them moving, stopping and starting again across the whole scene.
The event itself. The manuscript is explicit that the sound does not fade or muffle, it ceases, so the asset has to end in real silence rather than a tail.
The other half of the event. These two are always used as a pair, with the silence between them carried by the manifest's own pause rather than by either file.
The shake that makes Sarah catch herself against the console. Used where the manuscript shakes the building, not as general tension.
Jack waking so hard the chair moves. It gives the alarm a physical consequence in a body rather than only on a screen.

Two people arranging themselves around one workstation. Used twice: Sarah pulling a second chair over, and Jack rolling sideways to make room. Consciously different from the fast roll -- that one is a startle, this one is a marriage.
The single biggest sound event in the chapter. The escalation from one chirp to this is the whole opening beat.
The polite tone that fails to wake Jack. Used twice in Chapter 1 -- the second, louder tone is this same asset at a higher gain, which is what the manuscript describes.

The unexplained vibration that arrives twice at the end of chapter 3 and that Jack decides he does not want to explain. The single most important new asset: it is the first sound of the giant world and it will recur for a long time.
The terminal undoing Jack's lock without being asked. Soft on purpose: a bang would make it an attack, and the point is that it is calm.

Sarah's gray sneakers, per Chapter 1 visual canon -- explicitly not heels. Used twice and only for spatial transitions: entering the laboratory, and crossing the room to Jack. The listener never hears her walk otherwise.
Closes the frame the intercom opened. Without it the listener has no cue that the channel is gone, and the room's silence afterward is part of the scene.
Marks the acoustic frame Sarah's remote voice arrives in. Used twice: reaching for the intercom, and tapping the button again.
The manuscript makes static the ANSWER to Jack's question, so this is dialogue's turn in the scene, not decoration.
Used three times, only where the manuscript actually starts or resumes typing. It marks who has the keyboard, which is how the scene's authority shifts from Jack to Sarah.
Someone entering behind Jack while he is looking the other way. Pure spatial information, and the manuscript puts it mid-sentence on purpose.
Jack's physical shutdown. It has to sound conclusive, because the room coming back on afterwards is the moment TOMBS stops being a malfunction.
Deliberately calm. The unsettling thing about TOMBS opening its own directory is how unbothered it sounds. Used twice: the directory opening itself, and the file opening itself.
Jack taking control back. It has to sound like it worked, so that the terminal coming back on by itself lands as a violation.
Jack's wrist terminal, which carries every call with Lena across chapters 2 and 3. It needs to read as a different device from the laboratory console.
